experience.title: Vice President, Global Systems Engineering & Managed Services
experience.context: Recruited by the PE owner into a financially pressured $400M+ global satellite managed-services operation running across three regions, each operating differently. outcomes.claim: Stabilized the operation and built an automated Quote-to-Cash / RevOps model (ServiceNow + Microsoft Dynamics 365) that compressed order-to-delivery from weeks/months to days/weeks, which he credits with driving ~20% revenue growth on flat headcount and a ~20-point NPS improvement.
The business unit was successfully spun out / exited by the equity owner in 2026 following the automation and simplification work.

trajectory.arc: From individual-contributor engineer to VP/executive across 25-30 years in telecom (voice/TDM→IP, broadband/FTTH, satellite managed services, AI-ready infrastructure). dimensions.profile: Ramps by listening first and acting later. Walking into Speedcast — a domain (satellite) he knew at the fringes but not intrinsically — his first 30 days were deliberately about absorbing context: sitting one-on-one with each regional leader AND the teams to hear the challenges from both sides of the coin, mind-mapping where he sat, and looking for patterns to find low-hanging fruit he could tie to a quick, visible milestone. He explicitly framed the value of arriving as 'a new set of eyes' not yet clouded by living in the box.

stories.prompt: Take me back to your actual first 30 days at Speedcast — the literal daily behavior.
stories.narrative: New to satellite, he spent the first 30 days listening more than acting: one-on-ones with each leader and the teams to hear challenges from their eyes, finding patterns in the data, taking emotion out to see the gaps objectively, and building rapport/trust so people would open up about what was really broken. He credits this listen-first approach to his military background and upbringing, and says it got the org into cadence and results faster.

dimensions.self_report: Believes in a 30/60/90 approach; sees himself as arriving humble and listening before acting.

dimensions.profile: Verbally fluent and expansive — he thinks and persuades out loud, in ecosystem-level narrative. He named his own Achilles' heel candidly: taking that articulation and structuring it 'on paper' — a PowerPoint, a Word doc, a spreadsheet — is his weakest point, something he'd historically route around by pairing with teammates strong at it. The interviewer observed the same live: asked for a single pinned-down figure, his answers widened back into the market story rather than landing on one number.

stories.prompt: Name the specific kind of work that drained you — the actual task.
signals: weak on written/structured artifacts by his own account
stories.narrative: He said his Achilles' heel is when someone asks 'can you put that on paper / give me a presentation / structure that out.' He'd navigate around it by finding teammates who could construct documents while he collaborated verbally, and noted AI tooling has recently reduced this pain. He also admitted administrative overhead across fractured enterprise systems drained and stressed him.

dimensions.self_report: Describes himself as naturally strong at communicating, speaking, collaborating and evangelizing the art of the possible; openly admits paper/presentation work is his weakest area.

dimensions.profile: With customers, peers and reports he handles conflict by persuasion and patient re-framing — leaning into the vision, admitting when pieces aren't built yet, and staying focused on the customer's future-state outcome (the Brightspeed TR-069/Axon fight). With senior leadership whose direction diverges from his convictions, the pattern is different: twice he ultimately exited rather than fall in line — disagreeing with CTO Amir Hussein's 2016 pivot back to copper/DSL, and leaving Lumen in 2026 when he judged incoming leadership was short-sighting the strategy.

stories.prompt: Tell me about a time your team pushed back hard on one of your ideas.
stories.narrative: During Brightspeed, incoming Lumen traditionalists and a competitor (Axon) pushed to keep a legacy DSL base on old protocols and build a separate box. He fought through the headwinds by helping the CTO and customer see the unification/TCO benefit of one cloud-native control umbrella, admitting some development was still to come but keeping them focused on the forward framework. He frames it as taking 'broad shoulders' to stay the course.

stories.prompt: Last time you disagreed with your boss about something that mattered: what did you do?
signals: exits rather than conforms when senior leadership diverges from conviction
stories.narrative: In 2016 a new CTO steered CenturyLink back toward copper/DSL (a ~$2B program) away from fiber/PON. He disagreed ethically, felt the direction was stagnating the business against MSO competitors, and — after concluding the leader would never align — decided it was time to move on, which led to his Calix role.

dimensions.self_report: Describes himself as collaborative, humble, someone who listens and works shoulder-to-shoulder.

dimensions.profile: Has genuinely internalized at least one hard piece of feedback — that he doesn't need to be the smartest or most hands-on person in the room — and describes a real shift from engineer-doing to leader-mentoring/delegating. But under direct challenge in this interview about the vision-vs-specifics gap, he became somewhat defensive, characterizing those who want exact figures as 'number people' before returning to his narrative — so the humble self-image and the in-the-moment response to pointed feedback don't fully match.

stories.prompt: What's the hardest feedback you've ever gotten, and what changed after?
stories.narrative: The feedback was 'you don't have to be the smartest person in the room.' As an engineer he wanted hands on things; he learned in leadership to step back, trust and coach people who could be smarter than him, and stay in his swim lane. He ties this to valuing feedback loops (and to his intent-based feedback-loop patent).

stories.prompt: For a hiring manager, what should they make of the gap between sweeping vision and pinned-down specifics?
signals: reframes rather than concedes the gap
stories.narrative: Pressed on why precise numbers kept widening into narrative, he cited NDA/public-filing limits, restated the $450M and 35% figures, and argued that progress is 'a multitude of things' you can't pin to one finger — adding that 'people ask for specific numbers because all they are is number people' before reframing around outcome-backward thinking.

dimensions.self_report: Sees himself as humble, self-aware and coachable; someone who learned to let others shine.

dimensions.profile: Outcome-backward and vision-led. He repeatedly describes starting from the customer's/business's desired outcome and then 'backing into what needs to be true' to get there, rather than starting from mechanics — the through-line he calls the source of his success across his career.

stories.prompt: Walk me through the shape of your career the way you'd tell it to a friend.
stories.narrative: He frames his approach as aligning to the outcomes enterprises want and letting an AI framework (or a technical/commercial plan) derive the how — people become orchestrators of outcomes rather than doers of process. He consistently starts from 'what are they trying to achieve and what are the barriers' before building the commercial/technical/partnership motion.

dimensions.self_report: Describes himself as innovative-mindset-first, art-of-the-possible, seeing the forest for the trees.

dimensions.profile: Energized by customer-facing evangelizing, unlocking a customer's vision, mentoring/coaching leaders, and being on the innovative edge; drained by producing written/structured artifacts and administrative overhead across fragmented enterprise systems. He is explicit that he does his best work when he's a considered decision-maker at the table, not a transactional component.

stories.prompt: Name the specific kind of work that drained you.
signals: fueled by customer engagement and mentoring
wants to operate at strategic/decision level
stories.narrative: He named documentation/presentations and administrative work as the tasks that stressed and drained him and where he was least well-used, contrasted against the customer engagement, evangelizing and mentoring that fill his tank.

dimensions.self_report: Says he thrives on the challenge of helping customers unlock potential end-to-end and loves to mentor and coach.

dimensions.profile: Wants meaningful autonomy and to be a genuine consideration in decisions — he's clear he's demotivated by transactional roles and motivated by being valued for what he brings. He also describes having deliberately learned to give autonomy to his teams, trusting side-by-side and reporting talent to execute rather than doing the work himself.

stories.prompt: What are you actually looking for right now?
stories.narrative: He wants a full-time role that inspires innovation and growth, keeps him customer-engaged, and treats him as a consideration factor in decisions rather than a transactional component — noting he's lost patience with 'a digital wall in the middle' of hiring.

dimensions.self_report: Loves being a leader and mentor but says an IC/forward-delivery role also appeals; wants to be trusted and valued, not micromanaged into transactional work.

dimensions.profile: Under hard-deadline, cross-functional pressure he positions himself as the calm de-escalator and decision-forcer — stepping in front of frustration, forcing an A-vs-B call so the group can move on, and 'herding cats' toward the goal. He owns that the Speedcast crunch involved long, intense days and arguments, and that they hit the goal but not always as fast as hoped.

stories.prompt: The last week or two before Speedcast's hard deadline — hour to hour, what did it look like?
signals: de-escalates and forces decisions under pressure
stories.narrative: Days were long and intense with cross-functional arguments; he describes leaning in to say 'it's okay,' quickly sizing up options A and B and their deficits, making a collective decision and moving on — managing day-to-day operations in parallel with building the new operating model under equity-partner pressure. He frames it as needing broad shoulders and laser focus, everyone on the same sheet of music.

dimensions.self_report: Describes himself under pressure as having broad shoulders, staying laser-focused and stepping up to herd the cats.

manager_manual.feedback: Be direct and specific, and tie it to strategy and ethics — that's the language he respects. He genuinely absorbs developmental feedback about stepping back and empowering others. But note: when challenged head-on about the gap between his sweeping narrative and hard specifics, he can get defensive and reframe rather than concede. Ask for the precise number or artifact plainly and early, and give him room to come back with it rather than expecting it live.
manager_manual.check_ins: He does best with outcome-oriented check-ins and clear milestones, plus a strong feedback loop he can iterate against. Don't manage him through paperwork-heavy status reporting; that's his stated drain zone.
manager_manual.motivators: Customer engagement, evangelizing the art of the possible, being on the innovative edge, mentoring and building successor leaders, and being treated as a genuine decision-maker at the table.
manager_manual.onboarding: Give him a customer-facing, outcome-owning mandate on day one, not a documentation queue. He ramps by listening: expect his first 30 days to be one-on-ones with leaders and teams, pattern-finding and rapport-building before he restructures anything (as he did at Speedcast). Point him at a real problem statement and the desired business outcome and let him back into the plan.
manager_manual.demotivators: Transactional roles where he's a component not a voice; heavy documentation/PowerPoint/admin work; leadership he judges to be short-sighting the strategy or racing to speeds-and-feeds. He will disengage — and historically exit — when senior direction persistently conflicts with his convictions.
manager_manual.communication: Lean on him for live, synchronous, relational communication — that's where he's strongest. Pair him with someone who can convert his verbal vision into crisp written/structured artifacts (or expect AI tooling to fill that gap); don't make polished decks his primary deliverable.
